                                                    LIOUVILLE THEOREMS AND UNIVERSAL ESTIMATES
                                                         FOR SUPERLINEAR ELLIPTIC PROBLEMS
                                                             WITHOUT SCALE INVARIANCE

                                                                   PAVOL QUITTNER(1) AND PHILIPPE SOUPLET(2)




arXiv:2407.04154v2 [math.AP] 26 Sep 2024
                                                   Abstract. We give applications of known and new Liouville type theorems to universal
                                                   singularity and decay estimates for non scale invariant elliptic problems, including Lane-
                                                   Emden and Schrödinger type systems. This applies to various classes of nonlinearities
                                                   with regular variation and possibly different behaviors at 0 and ∞. To this end, we
                                                   adapt the method from [72] to elliptic systems, which relies on a generalized rescaling
                                                   technique and on doubling arguments from [55].
                                                      This is in particular facilitated by new Liouville type theorems in the whole space and
                                                   in a half-space, for elliptic problems without scale invariance, that we obtain. Our results
                                                   apply to some non-cooperative systems, for which maximum principle based techniques
                                                   such as moving planes do not apply. To prove these Liouville type theorems, we employ
                                                   two methods, respectively based on Pohozaev-type identities combined with functional
                                                   inequalities on the unit sphere, and on reduction to a scalar equation by proportionality
                                                   of components.
                                                      In turn we will survey the existing methods for proving Liouville-type theorems for
                                                   superlinear elliptic equations and systems, and list some of the typical existing results
                                                   for (Sobolev subcritical) systems.
                                                      In the case of scalar equations, we also revisit the classical Gidas-Spruck integral
                                                   Bernstein method, providing some improvements which turn out to be efficient for certain
                                                   nonlinearities, and we next compare the performances of various methods on a benchmark
                                                   example.
                                                      AMS Classification: Primary: 35J60; 35J47. Secondary: 35B45; 35B40; 35B53.
                                                      Keywords: Nonlinear elliptic systems, Liouville-type theorem, universal bounds,
                                                   decay, singularity estimates

                                           1. Introduction
1.1. Background and motivation. The present paper is concerned with Liouville type
theorems and universal estimates for elliptic problems, especially systems. Throughout
this paper, by a solution we mean a nonnegative strong solution1, unless otherwise speci-
fied. To begin with, denoting the Sobolev exponent by
                                        n+2
                                      (
                                            , if n ≥ 3
                                 pS = n−2
                                        ∞,     if n ≤ 2,
let us first recall the celebrated Gidas-Spruck elliptic Liouville theorem [38] (see also [10]
for a simplified proof).
Theorem A. Let 1 < p < pS . Then the equation
                                                −∆u = up                                                (1.1)
has no nontrivial solution in Rn .
The exponent pS is critical for nonexistence since, as is well known, there exist positive
solutions of (1.1) in Rn whenever n ≥ 3 and p ≥ pS (see [64, Section 9] and the references
therein; the solution can even be taken bounded and radial). Concerning Liouville type
theorems for semilinear equations with more general nonlinearities, let us mention the
following important generalization of Theorem A, due to [46].
Theorem B. Assume that f ∈ C([0, ∞)), with f (s) > 0 for all s > 0 and, if n ≥ 3,
                           s−pS f (s) is nonincreasing and nonconstant.                                 (1.2)
Then the equation
                                       −∆u = f (u),          x ∈ Rn                                     (1.3)
has no nontrivial solution.
   Elliptic Liouville theorems, in combination with rescaling techniques, have many appli-
cations. Theorem A (and its half-space analogue) was used in [39], as well as in many
subsequent papers, to show a priori bounds and existence for elliptic Dirichlet prob-
lems. In [55], by combining the rescaling method with a doubling argument, it was
shown that the Liouville property in Theorem A leads to universal estimates for singu-
larities and decay in unbounded domains. Liouville type theorems and their applications
have been extended in various directions, for instance systems or quasilinear problems
(cf., e.g., [31, 66, 69, 55, 70, 64, 52] and the references therein, and see also subsection 1.2
below).
   In [72] (see also [37] for a first step in that direction) was investigated the possibility, in
connection with Liouville type theorems, to generalize rescaling methods so as to obtain
a priori bounds and universal singularity or decay estimates for elliptic (and parabolic)
equations which are not scale invariant, even asymptotically, and whose behavior can be
quite far from power-like. This led to several natural classes of nonlinearities, including
   1                  2,r
    Namely, u ∈ Wloc       for all r ∈ (1, ∞) and the equation is satisfied a.e. Moreover, when boundary
conditions are imposed, a strong solution is assumed to be continuous up the boundary. Of course strong
solutions are classical if the nonlinearity is locally Hölder continuous (which we do not assume in general).
                        LIOUVILLE THEOREMS FOR ELLIPTIC PROBLEMS                            3

nonlinearities with regular variation, and motivated the need for further Liouville type
theorems for equations with nonhomogeneous nonlinearities. Let

                          f ∈ C([0, ∞)) with f (s) > 0 for all s > 0,                   (1.4)

and recall that f has regular variation at ∞ (resp., 0) with index q ∈ R if
                                                            L(λs)
               L(s) := s−q f (s) satisfies      lim               = 1 for each s > 0.   (1.5)
                                                 λ→∞
                                             (resp., λ→0)
                                                            L(λ)

Such functions L include, for instance, logarithms and their powers and iterates (see, e.g.,
[72, Section 2.3] for more examples). In particular the following connection was obtained
in [72] between Liouville theorems and universal bounds, extending [55] to semilinear
elliptic equations without scale invariance.

Theorem C. Assume (1.4). Suppose that

                   −∆v = f (v) has no nontrivial bounded solution in Rn                 (1.6)

and
                 f has regular variation at 0 and ∞ with indices in (1, pS ).           (1.7)
There exists a constant C = C(n, f ) > 0 such that, for any domain Ω ⊂ Rn and any
solution of −∆u = f (u) in Ω, we have the estimate
                           f (u(x))         C
                                    ≤     2        ,          for all x ∈ Ω.            (1.8)
                             u(x)     dist (x, ∂Ω)

   One of the aims of the present paper is to develop such tools and estimates for non
scale-invariant elliptic systems. We will take this opportunity to summarize and compare
the various existing methods to prove Liouville-type theorems for elliptic equations and
systems.
   A second motivation is the companion paper [65], where we develop similar ideas for
parabolic problems. Since we use there the approach from [59, 60, 61], which enables one
to derive parabolic from elliptic Liouville theorems, this will be facilitated by the results
in the present paper.
   Specifically, we shall consider elliptic systems of the form

                                   −D∆U = f (U ),            x ∈ Rn ,                   (1.9)

where n ≥ 2, m ≥ 1, D is an m × m diagonal matrix with positive (constant) entries
di > 0, U : Rn → Rm , f ∈ C(Rm ; Rm ) and where we denote ∆U = (∆u1 , . . . , ∆um )T .
The components of f will be denoted by fi . We shall also consider the corresponding
half-space problem
                                                x ∈ Rn+ ,
                          (
                            −D∆U = f (U ),
                                                                               (1.10)
                                 U = 0,        x ∈ ∂Rn+ ,
where Rn+ := {x = (x1 , . . . , xn ) ∈ Rn : xn > 0}.
4                             PAVOL QUITTNER AND PHILIPPE SOUPLET

1.2. A brief survey of existing methods and results. We first give a brief survey
of existing methods for proving Liouville-type theorems for superlinear elliptic equations
and systems (we warn the reader that our list of references is not exhaustive).
    • Scalar equations: whole space
    (a1) Integral Bernstein method (nonlinear integral estimates obtained by using Boch-
         ner’s identity, power change of dependent variable, and multipliers involving powers
         of u and cut-offs), and its variants [38, 10, 7, 8]
    (a2) Direct Bernstein method (application of the maximum principle to auxiliary func-
         tionals involving the unknown function and its gradient) [47, 43, 7, 34, 8, 49]
    (a3) Moving planes methods
       (a3.1) via symmetry, using the Kelvin transform [15, 6]
       (a3.2) moving spheres [46]
    • Scalar equations: half-space
    (b1) Moving planes methods
       (b1.1) via symmetry and reduction to a one-dimensional problem on a half-line,
              sometimes using the Kelvin transform [39, 4, 33]
       (b1.2) via monotonicity in the normal direction and reduction to an (n − 1) di-
              mensional problem in the whole space, sometimes using notions of stability
              [18, 4, 26, 28]
       (b1.3) via monotonicity and convexity in the normal direction, sometimes using no-
              tions of stability [16, 25]
    (b2) Stability estimates, combined with rescaling and monotonicity formulas [24]
    • Systems: whole space
    (a1) Integral Bernstein method [9]
    (a3) Moving planes methods
       (a3.1) via symmetry, sometimes using the Kelvin transform [32, 75, 41]
       (a3.2) moving spheres [66, 12, 76]
    (a4) Pohozaev-type identities combined with functional inequalities on the unit sphere2
         [68, 70, 53, 63, 71, 2, 29, 30, 54, 44, 21, 74]
    (a5) Reduction to a scalar equation by proportionality of components [48, 62, 17, 51, 27]
    • Systems: half-space
    (b1) Moving planes methods
       (b1.2) via monotonicity in the normal direction and reduction to an (n − 1) dimen-
              sional problem in the whole space [11]
       (b1.3) via monotonicity and convexity in the normal direction [16]
       (b1.4) moving spheres [66]
    (b3) Reduction to whole space by a Harnack inequality, a doubling argument and vari-
         ational identities [19, 20]
    (b4) Reduction to a scalar equation by proportionality of components [48, 51]

    2This method also works for scalar equations, but its primary interest is for systems.
                        LIOUVILLE THEOREMS FOR ELLIPTIC PROBLEMS                              5

Remark 1.1. (i) Some other methods are suitable for elliptic inequalities, but usually
require non-optimal growth restrictions on the nonlinearity when one considers equations.
Let us mention the rescaled test-function method (see [50] and, e.g., [64, Theorem 8.4])
and the spherical maximum method (see [1] and [64, Remark 8.5a(ii)] and the references
therein). Also one can sometimes prove a Liouville theorem by reducing to the radial case
after applying a symmetry result in the whole space based on moving planes (see, e.g., [13]).
   (ii) Some other methods apply to special classes of solutions, such as stable solutions or
solutions stable outside of a compact (see [26] and [64, Remark 8.5(vi)] and the references
therein). See also [64, Appendix H] for some other, more specific, methods. Also, there
are other methods which essentially apply to dissipative nonlinearities or nonlinearities
with sublinear or linear growth at infinity. We will not discuss them, since we are mainly
interested in (non-dissipative) superlinear problems.
  Let us next mention some of the typical existing results of Liouville type for (Sobolev
subcritical) superlinear systems in the whole space.
  One of the best understood cases is that of subcritical cooperative nonlinearities, namely
those such that
   t → t−pS f (tu) is > 0 nonincreasing in [0, ∞) component-wise for each u ∈ (0, ∞)m .
In particular the results in [31, 66, 76], obtained by moving planes or moving spheres
methods (a3), give a fairly complete picture for that class (some special cases have also
been treated by the method (a1) in [9]).
  The following class of Schrödinger type nonlinearities has also received a lot of attention:
                                         βij uqi uq+1
                                   X
                         fi (u) =                 j ,  i = 1, . . . , m                  (1.11)
                                    1≤i,j≤m

with q > 0, βij ∈ R (note that this is a scale-invariant problem). While the cooperative
case (i.e. βij ≥ 0 for i 6= j) is essentially covered by [66, 76] (in the subcritical range
2q + 1 < pS ), the noncooperative cases are only partially understood and depend on
delicate properties of the interaction matrix (β). Optimal results (in the full Sobolev
subcritical range) for m = 2 and low dimensions were obtained in [63] by the method (a4),
which strongly relies on the variational structure of the problem. Some noncooperative
cases, as well as other systems involving sums and/or products of powers3, have been
treated in the full Sobolev subcritical range by the method (a5) in [48, 62, 51], and in the
half-space case by the method (b3) in [20]. Other Liouville-type results for (1.11) can be
found in, e.g., [19, 73, 71] (but they do not cover the full Sobolev subcritical range).
   Another system of particular interest, as a model of Hamiltonian (as opposed to gradi-
ent) system, is the Lane-Emden system −∆u = v p , −∆v = uq . Although cooperative, a
significant difficulty is that the two equations have different degrees of homogeneity, and
the Sobolev subcritical condition is given by a hyperbola in (p, q). Several results have
been obtained by methods (a3) and (a4) – see Remark 4.1(i) below for details.
Remark 1.2. (i) The method of Pohozaev-type identities combined with functional in-
equalities on the unit sphere (a4) doesn’t seem to have been considered for non scale in-
variant problems nor for half-spaces so far. As we will see, it will turn out to be applicable,
after some modifications, and lead to some new Liouville-type theorems for systems. We
  3possibly noncooperative and nonvariational, including some Lotka-Volterra type systems
6                         PAVOL QUITTNER AND PHILIPPE SOUPLET

will also study the application to non scale invariant systems of the method of proportion-
ality of components (cf. (a5)-(b4)), which was so far mostly considered for scale invariant
nonlinearities.
   (ii) On the contrary, the Bernstein methods (a1)-(a2) do not seem to be applicable to the
half-space case. This may be due to the fact that, in order for them to be applied with full
efficiency, one has to use negative powers of u as new variable and/or test function, which
may cause substantial difficulties near the boundary. As for the method (b2) for systems
in the half-space, it seems to depend on scale invariance in an essential way. Finally the
direct Bernstein method (a2) does not seem to have been studied for systems.
   (iii) The optimality of the subcriticality condition for the Liouville property in the scalar
case (cf. after Theorem A) has a natural counterpart in many systems. However, as an
interesting difference, whereas any entire solution of the scalar equation (1.1) in the critical
case p = pS is known to be radially symmetric (cf. [14]), the symmetry property may fail
in the case of systems with critical nonlinearities of the form (1.11) (see [40]).
1.3. Outline. Section 2 is devoted to our new Liouville type theorems. In Subsection 2.1
and 2.2, we will give Liouville type theorems for non scale invariant systems, both in the
whole space and in the half-space, obtained respectively by the method (a4), based on
Pohozaev identities and functional inequalities on the unit sphere, and by the method
(a5)-(b4), based on of proportionality of components. In Subsection 2.3, we will get back
to the case of scalar equations and (mildly) revisit the classical Gidas-Spruck integral
Bernstein method (a1), providing some improvements which turn out to be efficient for
certain nonlinearities. In Section 3 we will compare the performances of several methods
on a benchmark scalar example. In Section 4 we will give applications of known and
new Liouville type theorems to universal bounds for singularity and decay estimates.
This will concern non scale invariant systems with nonlinearities having regular variation,
either with different indices on the components (Lane-Emden type systems), or with equal
indices. In Section 5 we will prove Theorem 2.1 and also provide some additional properties
of possible independent interest. The remaining sections will be devoted to the proofs of
the other resuts. Finally some properties of regularly varying functions will be given in
appendix.

                               2. Liouville type theorems
2.1. Method of Pohozaev identities and functional inequalities on the unit
sphere. We assume that the system has gradient structure, i.e.
                        f = ∇F, for some function F ∈ C 1 (Rm , R).                       (2.1)
Fixing p ≥ q > 1, we next assume that, for each M > 0, there exist constants cM , CM > 0
such that the functions f and F satisfy the following conditions:
                           |f (U )| ≤ CM |U |q , for all U ∈ [0, M ]m ,                   (2.2)

              2nF (U ) − (n − 2)U · ∇F (U ) ≥ cM |U |p+1 , for all U ∈ [0, M ]m .         (2.3)
For some results we also assume that there exist constants ξ ∈ (0, ∞)N and cM > 0 such
that
                          ξ · f (U ) ≥ cM |U |p , for all U ∈ [0, M ]m .                  (2.4)

satisfied and U is a bounded solution of (1.9) or (1.10), then U ≡ 0.

Remark 2.1. If we only consider radial solutions of (1.9), then using the same argu-
ments as in the proof of [63, Proposition 5(i)] one can show that the condition p < p∗ in
Theorem 2.1 can be replaced with p < pS .
   As a first application of Theorem 2.1, we have the following result concerning nonco-
operative, multi-power Schrödinger type systems, which arise in models of Bose-Einstein
condensates (see [36, 42]). Liouville theorems for systems of this type were established
in [19, 73, 63, 71] under various assumptions ([19, 73] being restricted to systems with
single power homogeneity). Corollary 2.1 directly follows from Theorem 2.1 by taking
p = q = α. We note that Corollary 2.1 for Ω = Rn could be deduced from [63, Theorem 4]
at the expense of a bit of additional work, but the case Ω = Rn+ is completely new.

Remark 2.2. (a) In the half-space case, the condition p < n/(n − 2) is better than the
well-known condition p ≤ (n + 1)/(n − 1) for inequalities [5].
   (b) System (1.9) is not cooperative in general. Therefore, maximum principle tech-
niques, such as moving planes or moving spheres (see, e.g., [15, 32, 66, 12]), are not
applicable here.
   (c) The value of ε0 in Theorem 2.1 (also in Theorem 5.1 below) is explicit and could be
computed from the proof. However its expression is rather complicated.
   (d) By using some arguments from [63, 71], the boundedness hypothesis in Theorem 2.1
could actually be replaced with an exponential growth condition, provided we assume (2.3),
(2.4) with cM independent of M and
                                  |f (U )| ≤ c1 (|U |q + |U |p ),                        (2.9)
with some c1 > 0, instead of (2.2).
Remark 2.3. The logarithms in Corollary 2.2 could be replaced, under suitable assump-
tions on the parameters, by some more general slowly varying functions (cf. (1.5)), such
as iterated logarithms (see [72, Section 2.3] for more examples).

The following theorem guarantees the equality of components. It is a special case of a
result from [65], established there for parabolic systems. See [48, 62, 17, 51, 27] for results
of this type in the case of elliptic systems with power nonlinearities.

homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions if D = Rn+ . Then u ≡ v.

If (u, v) is a bounded solution of (2.10), with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions

Remark 2.4. (i) The assumption that φ ≥ cM > 0 for u, v ≤ M in Theorem 2.2 is not
technical, since (2.10) admits the semitrivial solution (u, v) = (0, C) whenever φ(0, C) = 0
for C > 0. Theorem 2.2 in Rn may even fail in the class of positive solutions when
φ(u, v) = up v p , k(s) = 1 and g(s) = sq (see [51, Theorems 2.1 and 2.4] for positive and
negative results depending on the values of p).
   (ii) The boundedness assumption in Theorems 2.2 and 2.3 is not purely technical either.
Indeed, consider φ ≡ 1, k(s) = sp and g(s) = sq , with q ≥ p > 0, p+q ≤ 1 and λ > 0. Then
assumptions (2.11)–(2.13) are satisfied but (2.10) admits unbounded solutions in D = Rn ,
or in D = Rn+ with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions, of the form (w, 0) and
(0, w) with w ≥ 0 nontrivial. Namely, for p + q < 1, w is given by w(x) = √           c|xn |a ,
a = 2/(1 − p − q) and some √  c = c(p, q, λ) > 0 and, for p + q = 1, by w(x) = cosh( λ xn )
if D = Rn and w(x) = sinh( λ xn ) if D = Rn+ .
   (iii) Under the assumptions of Theorem 2.3 with λ = 1, it follows that u is a bounded
harmonic function, hence u = v = C ≥ 0 in case D = Rn by Liouville’s Theorem, and
u = v = 0 in case D = Rn+ by Phragmen-Lindelöf ’s Theorem (see, e.g., [57]).
   (iv) Assumption (2.14) for D = Rn+ and n ≥ 2 can be replaced for instance by lim inf s→0+
s−(n+1)/(n−1) h(s) > 0 (see [1, Corollary 5.6]).
2.3. Modified Gidas-Spruck method. In this subsection we get back to the case of
scalar equations and (mildly) revisit the classical Gidas-Spruck method. It appears that
there is room for some improvements which will turn out to be efficient for certain non-
linearities (see Section 3). We thus consider the semilinear equation
                                         −∆u = f (u),     x ∈ Rn ,                         (2.15)
where
                 f : [0, ∞) → [0, ∞) is continuous, f (0) = 0 and n ≥ 3.                   (2.16)
Denote ω1 = (0, 1], ω2 = (1, ∞).
Theorem 2.4. Assume (2.16) and let
                                                             n
                              p1 , p2 ∈ (1, pS ),              .
                                                    0 < κ̄ < κ :=                          (2.17)

Remark 2.5. The classical Theorem A in Section 1.1 is a special case of Liouville type
theorems obtained in [38] for more general nonlinearities of the form f (x, u) (also on
Riemannian manifolds). In the Euclidean case with f = f (u), the Liouville type theorem
in [38, Theorem 6.1] requires that f ∈ C 1 ([0, ∞)) and that
                         s−p f (s) is nonincreasing for some p ∈ (1, pS )                      (2.20)
(plus some additional assumptions). Condition (2.20) is stronger than assumption (1.2) of
Theorem B, and (2.20) also implies (2.19) (see Lemma 2.1 below). We refer to Section 3
for further comparison on a benchmark example.

Lemma 2.1. Assume f ∈ C 1 ([0, ∞)) and (2.20). Then (2.19) is true for some κ̄ ∈ (0, κ).
Proof. We may assume p ∈ (κ − 1, pS ) without loss of generality (since (2.20) remains true
for any larger p < pS ). We have κ̄ := p + 1 − κ ∈ (0, κ). We may also suppose that
                                   Z 1
                                       σ −κ f (σ)dσ < ∞,                             (2.27)
                                           0

since otherwise φ(s) = ∞ for all s > 0 and there is nothing to prove. Then letting
h(s) := s1−κ f (s) − κ̄φ(s) for all s > 0, we have h ∈ C 1 (0, ∞) and assumption (2.20)
implies that
     h′ (s) = s1−κ f ′ (s) + (1 − κ − κ̄)s−κ f (s) = s−κ (sf ′ (s) − pf (s)) ≤ 0,     s > 0.   (2.28)
Since (2.27) guarantees that lim inf s→0 h(s) ≤ lim inf s→0 s1−κ f (s) ≤ 0, it follows from
(2.28) that h ≤ 0 on (0, ∞), hence (2.19).                                                

Remark 3.1. If u is a solution of (3.1)–(3.2), then v(x) := u( √1K x) is a solution of (3.1)

                             f (u) = (1 + a min(1, up−1 ))up ,                         (3.4)
where a = 1/K. Consequently, problem (3.1), (3.4) has an explicit positive solution if

suggests that the equations −∆u = up loga (2 + u) and −∆u = up log−a (2 + u−1 ) (which do
not possess nontrivial solutions for a > 0 small due to Theorem B) could possess positive
solutions for some a large enough.

3.2. Non open range for the Liouville property. In the case of scale-invariant prob-
lems, it is known that the Liouville property has an open range with respect to the
exponent (see [64, Proposition 21.2b and subsequent comments]).

invariance. Let n ≥ 3, κ = n−2  n

−∆u = fk (u) in Rn possess explicit bounded radial solutions uk = uk (|x|) satisfying
                                    2kpk ξk2                         n−2

(see [45]), but the limiting equation −∆u = f (u) with f (u) = uκ + upS does not possess
nontrivial solutions by Theorem B.
   On the other hand, assume that limλ→0+ ff(λs)                       f (λs)

                                         4. Universal bounds
    In this section, for systems with regularly varying nonlinearities, we will give applica-
tions of known and new Liouville type theorems to universal bounds for singularity and
decay estimates.
    Namely, we shall describe the connections between universal estimates of solutions of
an elliptic system with given nonlinearity f and the three natural associated Liouville
type properties. The latter, that we denote by LP, LP0 , LP∞ , mean the nonexistence
of nontrivial bounded entire solutions for the systems with nonlinearities f, f0 , f∞ , where
f0 , f∞ denote the generalized rescaling limits4 of f , respectively near 0 and ∞.

   4These limits can be defined in a vector-valued way, with a single index of regular variation (see
subsection 4.2), or component-wise, allowing different indices of regular variation (see subsection 4.1).
                         LIOUVILLE THEOREMS FOR ELLIPTIC PROBLEMS                                     13

  Stated in loose terms, under suitable assumptions, we have the implications:
           
            LP∞ =⇒ universal singularity estimates of all solutions
           
              LP     =⇒ universal decay without rate for bounded solutions                         (4.1)
           
            LP
                 0   =⇒ universal decay rates for small solutions.
Here singularity and decay will be expressed in terms of d−2 (x), as d(x) → 0 and ∞,
respectively, where d(x) is the distance to the boundary of the domain where the equation
is satisfied.5 Moreover, the above properties can be suitably combined to yield:
           LP & LP0       =⇒ universal decay rates for bounded solutions
           LP & LP0 & LP∞ =⇒ universal decay rates for all solutions.
  Before going to specific results, we record right away the following general proposition,
which describes the second implication in (4.1) (its proof will be rather simple, while the
other two will require more assumptions and more work).
Proposition 4.1. Let f : K → Rm be continuous, Λ > 0 and assume that the sys-
tem −∆V = f (V ) admits no nontrivial strong solution in Rn with kV k∞ ≤ Λ. Then
limR→∞ η(R) = 0, where6
               n
     η(R) = sup |U (x)|, Ω ⊂ Rn is open, U : Ω → K is a bounded strong solution
                                                                             o
                  of −∆U = f (U ), kU k∞ ≤ Λ and x ∈ Ω with dist(x, ∂Ω) ≥ R .

   We note that some connections of the above type were described for scalar equations
in [72, Section 4.2], but the extension to systems will require nontrivial additional argu-
ments. In the next two subsections, we will develop such considerations for non scale
invariant systems with regularly varying nonlinearities, either with different indices on the
components (Lane-Emden type systems), or with equal indices.

4.1. Lane-Emden type systems. We here study systems where the nonlinearities have
regular variation with different indices on the components. For simplicity we restrict
ourselves to the following non-scale invariant Lane-Emden type systems (more general
systems could be considered):
                                     (
                                       −∆u = f1 (v),
                                                                                 (4.2)
                                       −∆v = f2 (u),
which is a modification of the classical Lane-Emden system

                                       (

                                               −∆v = uq .
For p, q > 0, we consider nonlinearities f = (f1 , f2 ) satisfying the following, slightly
reinforced, regular variation assumptions:
             fi are continuous on [0, ∞), fi are C 1 and positive for s > 0 large,                 (4.4)

of bounded domains).

Remark 4.1. (i) The optimal condition on p, q > 0 for nonexistence of nontrivial solutions
of (4.3) on Rn is conjectured to be given by the so-called Lane-Emden hyperbola:
                                     1   1    n−2
                                       +    >                                             (4.8)
                                    p+1 q+1    n
or equivalenty α + β > n − 2 with α = 2(p+1)        2(q+1)
                                         pq−1 , β = pq−1 in the “superlinear” case pq > 1.
So far the conjecture has been fully established only for n ≤ 4. While the necessity of
condition (4.8) is known in any dimension, nonexistence for n ≥ 5 is known only under
some additional restrictions on p, q. For example, simple sufficient conditions in any
dimension are given by p, q ≤ pS with (p, q) 6= (pS , pS ), or max(α, β) ≥ n − 2. See [70]
and [64, Section 31.2] for details.
   (ii) In the special case of the Lane-Emden system (f1 (v) = v p , f2 (u) = uq ) and p, q > 1,
Theorem 4.1 was proved in [55]. Note that in that case, estimate (4.7) can be rewritten as
                           u1/α + v 1/β ≤ C(1 + d−1 (x)),        x ∈ Ω.

Remark 4.2. Theorem 4.3(iii) extends Theorem C to systems. More precisely, Theorem C
follows from Theorem 4.3(iii) with m = 1 by using the classical Liouville theorem in [38]
(and Lemma 8.1 below).
Remark 4.3. (A priori estimate for the Dirichlet problem) Under the hypotheses of The-
orem 4.3(i), assume in addition that Ω is uniformly regular of class C 2 , that U ∈ C(Ω)
satisfies the Dirichlet boundary conditions U = 0 on ∂Ω, and that the Liouville property
is also true in the half-space (i.e., the problem −∆V = f∞ (V ) does not possess nontrivial
bounded entire solutions V : Rn+ → K with V = 0 on ∂Rn+ ). Then there exists a constant
C = C(n, f, Ω) (independent of U ) such that |U (x)| ≤ C for all x ∈ Ω. This follows by
modifying the proof of Theorem 4.3(i) along the lines of the proof of [56, Theorem 4.1].
Remark 4.4. The third implication in (4.1) can be illustrated by the following variant
of Theorem 4.3(ii). Assume that f + (λ) > 0 for λ > 0 small and that (4.13) is satisfied,
where f0 is homogeneous of order q > 1. Assume also that the problem −∆V = f0 (V ) does
not possess nontrivial bounded entire solutions V : Rn → K. Then there exist constants
ε0 , C > 0, depending only on n, f , such that (4.14) holds in Ω̂ = {x ∈ Ω; |U (x)| ≤ ε0 }
(hence in particular in Ω for small solutions, namely if kU k∞ ≤ ε0 ). This follows from
straightforward modifications of the proof of Theorem 4.3(ii), where only the case mk → 0
will occur.

                                5. Proof of Theorem 2.1
5.1. A conditional Liouville theorem. Theorem 2.1 will be obtained as a consequence
of the following conditional Liouville theorem, which is an extension of [71, Theorem 2].
The necessary a priori integral estimate (5.2) to apply Theorem 5.1 will be given in Sub-
sections 5.4-5.5 below. In what follows we set BR = {x ∈ Rn : |x| < R}.
Theorem 5.1. Let p0 ∈ (1, p∗ ), s ≥ 1 and assume
                                          (n − 1)(p0 − 1)
                                     s>                   .                            (5.1)
                                                   2
There exists ε0 = ε0 (n, p0 , s) > 0 such that, if
                  p0 − ε0 ≤ q ≤ p ≤ p0 + ε0 ,        p ≥ s,   0 ≤ δ0 ≤ ε0 ,
(2.2)-(2.3) are satisfied and U ≥ 0 is a bounded solution of (1.9) or (1.10) verifying
                            Z
                                           n− 2s +δ
                                |U |s ≤ CR p−1 0 ,       R ≥ 1,                        (5.2)
                             BR
then U ≡ 0.

Remark 5.1. The quantity δ0 in (5.2) allows for a possible “defect of scale invariance”
caused by the gap between p and q in assumptions (2.2)-(2.3) (see (5.41) below). As for the
restrictions s ≤ p and s ≥ 1, they could be relaxed at the expense of further complications
in the proof, using additional arguments from [71]. We have refrained from expanding on
this since we always have s ∈ [1, p] in our applications. Also, as in [71], we could handle
solutions with some exponential growth, provided we assume (2.3) with cM independent of
M , and (2.9) instead of (2.2), instead of just bounded solutions.
   The proof of Theorem 5.1 is long and technical. It relies on an extension of a feedback
procedure from [70, 63, 71]. More precisely, by means of a Rellich-Pohozaev type identity,
for any r > 0, the volume integral
                                          Z
                                 H(r) :=        |U |p+1 dx
                                             |x|<r

can be controled by surface integrals involving |U |p+1 , |∇U |2 and |U |2 at |x| = r. Fix
R > 0. If, for some r ∈ R, 2R , one can estimate these surface terms by CR−a H b (3R)
                                

with C, a > 0, b ∈ [0, 1) independent of R, then one easily infers that H(R) has very
fast growth as R → ∞, hence contradicting the boundedness assumption on U . It turns
out that such estimation can be achieved by a careful analysis using Sobolev imbeddings
and interpolation inequalities on S n−1 , elliptic estimates and a measure argument. In
this scheme, the primary integral bound (5.2) is used in the interpolation step, where
the surface terms are interpolated between various auxiliary norms. Heuristically, the
efficiency of the method comes from the fact that one space dimension is “gained” via
the Pohozaev type identity because, by applying functional analytic arguments on the
20                        PAVOL QUITTNER AND PHILIPPE SOUPLET

n − 1 dimensional unit sphere rather than directly on BR , one can bootstrap from (5.2)
under less stringent growth restrictions on the nonlinearity. Related arguments, without
interpolation and feedback, and restricted to n = 3, first appeared in [69]. Both [69]
and [70] were exclusively concerned with the Lane-Emden system −∆u = v p , −∆v = uq .
Although many parts are similar to the proofs in [70, 63, 71], it requires many nontrivial
changes and we give a complete proof for self-containedness.

  Step 8. Conclusion. Inequalities (5.5), (5.6), Lemmas 5.9–5.10 and the nondecreasing
property of H imply that

                         H(R) ≤ C0 R−â H b̂ 3R , R ≥ R0 ,
                                                 
                                                                                (5.37)

for some constant C0 > 0, with â = min(a, ã′ ) > 0 and b̂ = max(b, b̃′ ) ∈ [0, 1). It can
be shown (see [71] for details) that (5.37) entails an exponential lower bound on H(R).
But the boundedness assumption on U implies H(R) = O(Rn ) as R > 1. This is a
contradiction and Theorem 5.1 is proved.

5.4. A priori estimates and proof of Theorem 2.1. It is well known (see, e.g., [63,
Lemma 3.4]) that, under assumption (2.4), any bounded solution of (1.9) satisfies (5.2)
with s = p, δ0 = 0 (and C depending on the bound of the solution). Theorem 2.1 in the
whole space case is then a direct consequence of Theorem 5.1.
   To prove Theorem 2.1 in the half-space case, we shall rely on the following a priori
estimate, whose proof is postponed to the next section.

Proof of Proposition 2.1. We show that there exists a radial, positive bounded solution of
−∆u = f (u) ≡ cg(u)g ′ (u) with c = 2(1 − λ), which will immediately provide a solution
(u1 , u2 ) = (u, u) of (1.9).
  To this end we use a small modification of Ran argument from [62, 72] (see [62, Theo-
                                                s
rem 1.4] and [72, Proposition 1]). Let H(s) = 0 f (z)dz and ψ(s) = sf (s) − (pS + 1)H(s).
We first claim that there exists s0 > 0 such that
                                  ψ(s) ≥ 0 for all s ∈ [0, s0 ].                          (5.63)
Indeed, we have g(s) ∼ sb+a as s → 0, with b = (p       0 + 1)/2 > 1. By (5.58) and the fact
that lims→0+ h1 (s) = 1, we deduce that g (s) ∼ (b + a)sb+a−1 , hence f (s) ∼ c̃s2(b+a)−1
                                            ′

with c̃ = (b + a)c. Consequently, H(s) ∼ (2(b + a))−1 c̃s2(b+a) and, since a > a0 = pS2+1 − b,
it follows that ψ(s) ∼ [1 − (pS + 1)(2(b + a))−1 ]c̃s2(b+a) > 0 as s → 0, hence (5.63).
  The end of the proof is then the same as in [72, Proposition 1], which we repeat for
convenience. Extend f by 0 for s < 0 and consider the initial value problem
                  −(r n−1 v ′ )′ = r n−1 f (v), r > 0,   v(0) = s0 ,    v ′ (0) = 0.
Let R∗ be its maximal existence time. Since f ≥ 0, we have v ′ ≤ 0 on [0, R∗ ). Assume for
contradiction that v has a (first) zero R ∈ (0, R∗ ). Then v is a solution of −∆v = f (v) on
the ball BR with Dirichlet boundary conditions and 0 ≤ v ≤ s0 . But in view of (5.63) and
                      LIOUVILLE THEOREMS FOR ELLIPTIC PROBLEMS                            41

Pohozaev’s inequality (see, e.g., [64, Corollary 5.2]), this is a contradiction. We conclude
that v > 0 on (0, ∞), which proves the desired result.                                    

                       6. Proof of Theorems 2.3, 2.4 and 2.5
Proof of Theorem 2.3. By Theorem 2.2, we have u = v and −∆u = (1 − λ)h(u). In the
case λ ∈ [0, 1), the conclusion then follows from Theorem B for D = Rn , and from [16] or
[25] for D = Rn+ .
   Let us consider the case λ > 1. Let M = 12 supD u ∈ [0, ∞) and assume for contradiction
that M > 0. Choose x0 ∈ D such that u(x0 ) ≥ M and, for any δ > 0, set uδ (x) =
u(x) − δ|x − x0 |2 . Since uδ (x) → −∞ as |x| → ∞ (and uδ < 0 on ∂D in case D = Rn+ ),
there exists xδ ∈ D such that uδ (xδ ) = sup uδ . Let τ = inf s∈[M,2M ] h(s) > 0. Since
u(xδ ) ≥ uδ (xδ ) ≥ uδ (x0 ) = u(x0 ) ∈ [M, 2M ], we have 0 ≥ ∆uδ (xδ ) = (λ − 1)h(u(xδ )) −
2nδ ≥ (λ − 1)τ − 2nδ > 0 for δ > 0 small: a contradiction.                                 

              7. Proof of Proposition 4.1, Theorems 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3
7.1. Proof of Proposition 4.1. Assume that the assertion fails. Then there exist δ > 0,
a sequence Rj → ∞ and solutions Uj of −∆Uj = f (Uj ) on BRj , such that kUj k∞ ≤ Λ
and |Uj (0)| ≥ δ. Since |f (Uj )| ≤ M := sup|ξ|≤Λ |f (ξ)| < ∞, it follows from interior elliptic
Lq estimates that some subsequence of Uj converges locally uniformly to a solution U∞ of
−∆U∞ = f (U∞ ) on Rn . Moreover, kU∞ k∞ ≤ Λ and |U∞ (0)| ≥ δ. This contradicts our
assumption.
7.2. Proof of Theorem 4.1. The proof of Theorem 4.1 is based on a doubling-rescaling
argument for systems from [55, Theorem 4.3], combined with the rescaling approach from
[72] for scalar problems with a regularly varying nonlinearity. However, it requires a rather
delicate rescaling procedure to handle regularly varying nonlinearities of different indices
in the two equations. To this end, for a given solution (u, v) of (4.2) in a domain Ω, we
shall introduce the key auxiliary function φ(N (u, v)), where

        8. Appendix: Some properties of regularly varying functions
  It is well known (see [67, Theorem 1.1]) that, for any regularly varying function of index
p ∈ R, the generalized rescaling limits are uniform on compact subsets of (0, ∞). We have
actually used the following lemma, which gives a stronger property: When p > 0, the
convergence is uniform on compact subsets of [0, ∞). This is probably known but we
haven’t found the result in the literature.
Lemma 8.1. Let f ∈ C([0, ∞)) and p > 0.
  (i) If f (s) > 0 for s > 0 large and lim ff(λs)    p

   Notice that f0+ (1) = 1 and f0+ is continuous, hence f0+ is positive on a neighborhood
of 1. Consequently, by standard results from regular variation theory (see, e.g., [67, The-
orem 1.3]), it follows from (7.38) that f+ has regular variation at 0, i.e. there exists q ∈ R
such that

                      L(s) = exp η(s) +      z −1 ξ(z) dz , s ∈ (0, Λ).
                                            1
As a consequence, we have log L(s) = o(| log s|) as s → 0, which readily implies (7.39). 
